definitions.type: family of metric topological spaces indexed by natural numbers
definitions.definition: For a natural number m, Eucl(m)=R^m is the space of real coordinate vectors indexed by {0,...,m-1}; distance between x and y is (sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(x_k-y_k)^2)^(1/2). The topology is generated by open balls for this distance. In particular Eucl(0) has exactly one vector, the empty tuple. Identify Eucl(m) × R with Eucl(m+1) by (x,t)↦(x_0,...,x_{m-1},t); its distance is sqrt(dist(x,y)^2+|t-u|^2), not the maximum product distance. Compact means that every cover by open sets has a finite subcover.

definitions.type: extended nonnegative real diameter of a subset of a metric space
definitions.definition: diam(A)=sup{dist(x,y): x,y∈A}, with diameter zero for A empty. For sets of finite diameter it is the usual nonnegative real diameter. All covers at a finite scale have finite diameters. For s>0 the cost of an empty set or a diameter-zero set is 0^s=0.

definitions.type: scale Hausdorff contents and Hausdorff measures on Euclidean subsets, valued in [0,∞]
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero.

Dimension inequalities against real numbers use their nonnegative extended-real values. Once finiteness has been proved the same symbols are also used for their real values.
F=E×I={(x,t):x∈E, t∈I}, using the coordinate-adjoining Euclidean identification of D001.
D=dim_H E. Its finiteness and bound by n are conclusions to be proved, not conditions of this definition.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on R with its Borel measurable structure
definitions.definition: λ denotes the standard Lebesgue measure on the Borel sigma algebra of R (used also as its outer measure on arbitrary sets). For a nonnegative Borel function, ∫ g dλ denotes its extended nonnegative Lebesgue integral. Indicator notation 1_T(t) is 1 for t∈T and 0 otherwise. A sum of nonnegative terms denotes the supremum of its finite partial sums and can equal infinity.

argument.text: Fix real s,δ and assume L1: s>0, δ>0. Put c=H^s_δ(E), finite by N001. Fix an arbitrary sequence V and assume L2: it is a δ-cover of F; finite countable covers can be padded by empty sets. Define ρ_i=diam(V_i), A_i and B_i as its first and last coordinate projections. The Euclidean distance formula gives coordinate distances at most the full distance, hence diam(A_i),diam(B_i)≤ρ_i≤δ. Fix ε and assume L3: ε>0. Define η_i=ε·2^(-i-1)/(1+ρ_i^s)>0. For nonempty V_i, B_i is nonempty and bounded (choose one of its points; every other is within δ). Its real infimum and supremum exist and sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i by the diameter bound. The open interval (inf B_i-η_i/2, sup B_i+η_i/2) contains B_i and has length ≤ρ_i+η_i. For empty V_i use the empty set instead. Thus the sequence of open enclosing intervals required in F001 exists. No measurability of V_i,A_i or B_i is asserted or needed.

produces.statement: There exists a sequence J such that if V_i is nonempty then J_i is a bounded open interval containing B_i with length at most ρ_i+η_i, and if V_i is empty then J_i is empty.

argument.text: Choose J from F001. For arbitrary t∈I and x∈E, (x,t)∈F, so some V_i contains (x,t). Then x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. Hence the A_i with t∈J_i cover E. They have diameter at most ρ_i≤δ; pad the remaining indices by empty sets. The definition of c as an infimum of cover costs gives c≤sum_i diam(A_i)^s 1_(J_i)(t)≤sum_i ρ_i^s 1_(J_i)(t). This proves F002 pointwise for all t∈I.

On all of R define f(t)=c·1_I(t) and g_i(t)=ρ_i^s·1_(J_i∩I)(t). F002 gives f≤sum_i g_i, including outside I where both sides vanish. Each J_i is open or empty and I is closed, so J_i∩I is Borel; the nonnegative constant indicators g_i are measurable and hence λ-almost everywhere measurable. Apply M002 to this pointwise inequality and M001 to the measurable nonnegative series. M003 evaluates the constant indicators, and M005 gives λ(I)=1. Thus c=cλ(I)=∫f dλ≤∫sum_i g_i dλ=sum_i∫g_i dλ=sum_i ρ_i^s λ(J_i∩I). By measure monotonicity and M006, λ(J_i∩I)≤λ(J_i)≤ρ_i+η_i (empty intervals have measure zero). It follows that c≤sum_i ρ_i^s(ρ_i+η_i)≤sum_i ρ_i^(s+1)+sum_i η_iρ_i^s≤sum_i ρ_i^(s+1)+ε, since η_iρ_i^s≤ε·2^(-i-1) and sum_{i≥0}2^(-i-1)=1. These inequalities of nonnegative series follow first for finite partial sums and then by their suprema. They include ρ_i=0 because s>0. No interchange of signed or nonmeasurable functions has occurred.

The bound F003 holds for every ε>0, with c and the original V,ρ fixed independently of ε. Discharge L3 and quantify ε. If sum_i ρ_i^(s+1)=∞ then c≤this sum immediately. If it is finite, any strict inequality c>sum_i ρ_i^(s+1) would be contradicted by choosing ε smaller than their positive difference. Thus c≤sum_i ρ_i^(s+1) in all cases. Discharge L2 and quantify V: every δ-cover of F has (s+1)-cost at least c.
